read.sections.0.heading.source: Stories move between words and images
read.sections.0.heading.back: Stories travel between words and pictures

read.sections.0.text.source:
A story can be spoken, written, performed or pictured. An artist chooses which moment to show, where to place the figures, and which details will help an audience recognise it. Knowing the story can change how we understand a picture. Looking at the picture can also show how a particular community presented that story at a particular time.

The two Thai panels in this lesson were made in the late nineteenth century. Both belong to a series about Prince Vessantara, a figure in a Buddhist Jataka story. It is a narrative, an account of connected events, and it is associated with generosity. The panels are painted on teak wood with a paint called glue tempera. The Walters Art Museum's records do not give the names of their makers. The story is older than the panels. Their date tells us when these works were made, not when the narrative began.
read.sections.0.text.note: Names in Thai script on purpose: เวสสันดรชาดก / พระเวสสันดร (Vessantara Jataka), สมัยรัตนโกสินทร์, ขรัวอินโข่ง, พระบาทสมเด็จพระจอมเกล้าเจ้าอยู่หัว (Mongkut). The checker warns that the Latin names are missing; these are real Thai names with standard Thai spellings, so the warning is expected. glossary "narrative" = เรื่องเล่า (not in KEY_TERMS; check).
read.sections.0.text.back:
A story may be told by mouth, written, performed or painted as a picture. An artist chooses which moment to show, where to place the figures, and what details to include to help the audience recognise the story. Knowing the story may change the way we understand the picture. Looking at the picture can also tell how one community presented that story at one particular time.

The two Thai panels in this lesson were made in the late 19th century CE. Both are part of a series of pictures of the story of Prince Vessantara, a character in a Jataka of Buddhism. This Jataka is a narrative, that is, a telling of connected events, and it is a story people associate with generosity and giving. The panels are painted on teak wood with a paint called glue-bound powder paint. The Walters Art Museum's records do not give the makers' names. This story is older than the pictures themselves. The year the pictures were made tells us when these works were made; it does not tell us when this narrative began.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A story can be told, written, acted or painted. An artist picks one moment to show. The artist picks details that help people know the story. Knowing the story helps us understand the picture. The picture also shows how one group told the story at one time.

The two Thai panels here were made in the late 1800s. Both are about Prince Vessantara. He is in a Buddhist story called a Jataka. It is a narrative. A narrative tells events that are linked. This one is about giving freely. The panels are paint on teak, a hard wood. The museum has no names for the painters. The story is much older than the panels. Their date tells us when they were made, not when the story began.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
A story can be told by mouth, written, performed or painted as a picture. The artist chooses one moment to paint. The artist chooses details that help people know which story it is. Knowing the story helps us understand the picture. The picture also tells how one group of people told this story at one time.

These two Thai panels were made in the late part of 1800 to 1899. Both panels tell the story of Prince Vessantara. Prince Vessantara is in a Buddhist story called a Jataka. This Jataka is a narrative. A narrative is the telling of events that follow on from each other. This story is about giving willingly. The panels are painted with paint on teak wood. Teak is a hard wood. The museum does not know the painters' names. This story is much older than the pictures. The year of the picture tells when the picture was made; it does not tell when the story began.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Two episodes from the same story

read.sections.1.text.source:
The panel called Chapter 2 shows the prince with a white elephant. The museum explains what happens at this point in the story. Visitors come from a neighbouring kingdom that is suffering from drought. They ask for the elephant, which brings rain. The Chapter 3 panel shows a later episode, or part of the story, with the prince's family and their chariot. These are episodes in a religious narrative. The rain-bringing animal and other extraordinary events belong to that narrative. They are not scientific or documentary claims.

An audience could connect the two scenes through familiar characters and the wider story. Setting, gesture, size and the arrangement of people help direct attention. One panel does not contain every event or explain every character. A series provides connections that a single image on its own may leave unclear.
read.sections.1.text.note: chariot = รถม้า (the picture shows a horse-drawn chariot; the Thai story says ราชรถ). Extraordinary events = เหตุการณ์อัศจรรย์; documentary claims = บันทึกเหตุการณ์จริง. Respectful wording of the religious story is worth a check by a Buddhist reader.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The panel called Chapter 2 shows Prince Vessantara with a white elephant. The museum explains what happens at this point in the story. Visitors come from a neighbouring kingdom that is suffering drought. They come to ask for this elephant, which can bring rain. The Chapter 3 panel shows a later episode, or part of the story: Prince Vessantara's family with their horse carriage. These events are episodes in a religious narrative. The animal that can bring rain and the other miraculous events are part of that narrative; they are not scientific claims or records of real events.

The audience can connect these two scenes through familiar characters and the whole story. Setting, gesture, size and the arrangement of people help lead the audience's eye. One panel alone does not contain every event or explain every character. A series of pictures helps connect what a single picture may leave unclear.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
In the Chapter 2 panel, the prince has a white elephant. The museum tells this part of the story. Visitors come from a nearby kingdom with no rain. They ask for the elephant. It brings rain. The Chapter 3 panel shows a later episode. An episode is one part of a longer story. It shows the prince's family and their chariot. A chariot is a kind of cart. An elephant that brings rain is part of a religious story. It is not a science fact or a news report.

People knew the story, so they could link the two scenes. Places, hand movements, size and where people stand guide our eyes. One panel does not show every event. A series of panels helps link them.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
In the Chapter 2 panel, Prince Vessantara is with a white elephant. The museum tells this part of the story. People come from a nearby kingdom where the rain does not fall. They come to ask for the elephant. This elephant can bring rain. The Chapter 3 panel shows a later episode. An episode is one part of a longer story. This picture has Prince Vessantara's family with a horse carriage. A horse carriage is a cart pulled by horses. The elephant that can bring rain is part of a religious story, not scientific truth or news.

People know this story, so they can connect the two scenes. The place, hand gestures, size and where people stand help guide our eye. One panel does not show every event. Several panels that make a series help join the story together.

read.sections.2.text.source:
Thailand's National Gallery gives another example of this changing artistic world. It identifies a different Vessantara panel by Khrua In-Khong. He was a Buddhist monk and a royal painter during King Mongkut's reign in the mid-nineteenth century. He adapted Western linear perspective, a way of suggesting depth, within Thai traditional painting. The Walters panels are not attributed to him. Still, his example helps explain the wider setting. Painters could keep a religious story while experimenting with how its world looked. Particular makers and patrons were actively developing Thai art.

The panels also tell us something about their own time. Their inscriptions, or writing placed on them, record that named donors commissioned them for religious purposes. To commission a work is to ask for it to be made. This connects each panel with patrons and community practice, even though the painter's name is unknown. The museum also discusses the shading and the space that seems to go back into the distance in the landscapes. It sees these as evidence of contact with European ways of painting. Local traditions could develop through exchange without losing every earlier feature.

Understanding these works brings several kinds of knowledge together: the story, the visible choices, how the panels were made, and their purpose. You do not need to share a belief to learn about its cultural and historical importance. Careful explanation treats the work's religious meaning with respect, while keeping evidence and interpretation apart.
read.sections.2.text.note: Royal words kept plain per KEY_TERMS: ในรัชสมัยพระบาทสมเด็จพระจอมเกล้าเจ้าอยู่หัว (standard), ช่างวาดของพระจอมเกล้าเจ้าอยู่หัว (simpler). linear perspective = ทัศนียภาพเชิงเส้นแบบตะวันตก (art teachers may say หลักทัศนียวิทยา). Pronoun for Khrua In-Khong avoided (a monk would usually be ท่าน, which the checker forbids), so his name is repeated.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Thailand's National Gallery gives another example of this changing art world. The Gallery identifies another panel of the Vessantara story painted by Khrua In-Khong. Khrua In-Khong was a Buddhist monk and a painter at the royal court in the reign of King Mongkut (Phra Bat Somdet Phra Chom Klao Chao Yu Hua), in the mid-19th century CE. Khrua In-Khong took Western linear perspective, a way of making a picture look deep, and adapted it within traditional Thai painting. The Walters museum's panels are not attributed to Khrua In-Khong. Still, this example helps explain the wider context. Painters could keep the religious story while experimenting with painting the story's world to look different. Some craftsmen and patrons were seriously developing Thai art.

These panels also tell us something about their own era. The inscription, or text written on the picture, records that donors whose names are given commissioned the pictures for religious use. To commission a work is to ask someone to create that work. This connects each panel with patrons and community practice, even though we do not know the painter's name. The museum also talks about the shading and the space that seems to go deep into the distance in the landscapes. The museum sees these as evidence of contact with European ways of painting. Local traditions could develop through exchange without having to lose all their earlier features.

Understanding these works means bringing several kinds of knowledge together: the story, what the craftsman chose to show, how the panels were made, and the purpose of the pictures. You do not need to share the same belief to learn about the cultural and historical importance of that belief. Careful explanation respects the religious meaning of the work and keeps evidence apart from interpretation.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Thailand's National Gallery has a different Vessantara panel. A monk named Khrua In-Khong painted it. He was also a painter for King Mongkut, in the mid-1800s. He used a Western way to show depth. The Walters panels are not by him. But his work shows that painters tried new ideas. They kept the old story but changed how its world looked.

The panels have inscriptions. An inscription is writing on an object. These say that named donors commissioned the panels for religious reasons. To commission a work means to ask for it. So we know who asked for them, even without the painters' names. The museum also points to shading and deep space in the landscapes. It says these show contact with European painting. Old ways could change and still keep many parts.

So we join the story and what we see. We add how and why the panels were made. Nobody has to share a belief to learn about it. We treat the religious meaning with respect. We keep what we see apart from what we think it means.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Thailand's National Gallery has another panel of the Vessantara story. A monk named Khrua In-Khong painted it. Khrua In-Khong was also King Mongkut's painter, in the middle part of 1800 to 1899. Khrua In-Khong used a Western method to make pictures look deep. The Walters panels are not Khrua In-Khong's work. But Khrua In-Khong's work tells us that painters tried new ideas. They kept the old story but changed how they painted the world in the story.

The panels have an inscription. An inscription is text written on an object. This inscription says that donors whose names are given commissioned the panels for religion. To commission a work is to ask someone to make a work for you. So we know who asked for the picture to be made, even though we do not know the painter's name. The museum also points out the shadows and the space that looks deep in the landscapes. The museum says this shows there was contact with European painting. Old ways can change and still keep many parts.

So we bring the story together with what we see, then add how the panels were made and what for. Nobody has to believe the same thing to learn about this. We respect the religious meaning of the picture. We keep what we see apart from what we think it means.

write.prompt.source: Explain how knowing the two episodes helps you understand these paintings. Use one detail from a panel and one fact about its past. Two or three sentences are enough.
write.prompt.back: Explain how knowing the story of these two episodes helps you understand these paintings. Use one detail from the panels and one fact about the pictures' past. Two or three sentences is enough.

write.sentenceStarters.0.source: In the panel, I can see ...

write.example.source: In the Chapter 2 panel, I can see the prince on a white elephant. Visitors kneel in front of him. The story tells me that they come from a kingdom with no rain. They ask for the elephant because it brings rain. The inscriptions show that named donors paid for the panels for religious reasons. So the picture shows one part of a well-known story, and its history tells us who supported it.
write.example.back: In the Chapter 2 panel, I see Prince Vessantara sitting on a white elephant, with visitors kneeling in front of him. The narrative tells me they come from a kingdom where the rain does not fall. They come to ask for the elephant because the elephant can bring rain. The inscription shows that donors whose names are given paid for the panel to be made for religion. So the picture shows part of a story people know well, and the picture's history also tells us who supported the making of this picture.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: The panels tell a Buddhist religious story. Teach it as a story with religious meaning, with respect. No learner is asked to accept or judge its moral lesson, to say what they believe, to share their own religion, or to take part in any practice. Keep to these two panels: don't expand the lesson into the more disturbing episodes elsewhere in the Vessantara story.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: These panels tell a Buddhist religious story. Teach it with respect as a story with religious meaning. Do not ask any learner to accept or judge the story's moral, say what they believe, tell about their own religion, or take part in any ceremony. Use only these two panels. Do not extend the lesson to other episodes of the Vessantara story that might be more upsetting.

educatorNotes.0.source: A historical artwork that depicts a story is not an eyewitness record of that story. Keep the painting's date (late nineteenth century) apart from the age of the story, and keep the extraordinary events of the narrative apart from documentary claims.
educatorNotes.0.back: Past artworks that show a story are not eyewitness records of that story. Separate the year the picture was painted (late 19th century CE) from the age of the story, and separate the miraculous events in the narrative from claims that record real events.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: a learner links something they can see (a figure, the elephant, the chariot) with the named episode, and adds information that the picture alone doesn't give: the order of the series, the donors' inscription, the date or the religious context. Don't require learners to endorse the story's moral lesson.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for the Write step: the learner connects something visible (the figures, the elephant or the carriage) with the named episode, and adds information the picture alone does not give, such as the order of the series, the donors' inscription, the year made or the religious context. Learners do not have to agree with the story's moral.

educatorNotes.2.back: Khrua In-Khong (from Thailand's National Gallery) is used for comparison only, to show the wider artistic context. educatorNotes.3.source: The Walters record of 35.233 has a gap in its ownership history before the donor collection; don't invent a complete history. The Met's resource Art of the Islamic World shaped the approach (context alongside close study of one illustrated object) but supplies none of the facts about these Thai works.

The Metropolitan Museum's (The Met) Art of the Islamic World resource is the model for the teaching method (studying context alongside close examination of one illustrated object) but gives no facts about these Thai works.
